claims.text: Under 28 days, all febrile infants: WBC with manual differential, blood cultures, urinalysis and urine culture by catheter, and CSF studies with culture and PCR as indicated.
claims.quote: All febrile children < 28 days require a white blood cell (WBC) count with a manual differential, blood cultures, urinalysis and urine culture (obtained by catheterization, not an external bag), and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) evaluation with culture and appropriate polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing (eg, for herpes simplex, enterovirus) as indicated by historical risk factors.

claims.text: CRP and/or procalcitonin can help gauge risk.
claims.quote: Inflammatory marker levels (C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, or both) may be measured to assist with risk assessment.

claims.text: Chest X-ray with respiratory signs; stool culture or enteric PCR with diarrhea.
claims.quote: Chest radiograph is done in neonates with respiratory manifestations. Stool is sent for culture or enteric PCR stool test in neonates with diarrhea.

claims.text: 1 to 3 months and ill-appearing or high risk: admit; WBC with manual differential, blood cultures, catheter urinalysis and urine culture, and lumbar puncture.
claims.quote: Febrile infants between 1 month and 3 months of age who are ill-appearing (eg, abnormal cry, lethargy, rectal temperature > 38.5° C) or who have risk factors for serious bacterial infection (eg, significant congenital anomalies, prematurity, technology dependence, unvaccinated) should be admitted to the hospital and have a WBC count with a manual differential, blood cultures, urinalysis and urine culture (obtained by catheterization, not an external bag), and lumbar puncture with CSF evaluation, including culture and, if available, PCR panel.

claims.text: Well-appearing, 29 to 60 days, low risk when all hold: rectal temperature ≤ 38.5° C, WBC 5,000 to 15,000/mcL with neutrophils ≤ 4000/mcL, procalcitonin ≤ 0.5 ng/mL and/or CRP ≤ 2 mg/dL, and a normal urinalysis.
claims.quote: Well-appearing febrile infants between 29 days and 60 days of age with all of the following are at low risk of serious bacterial infections: Rectal temperature ≤ 38.5° C Normal WBC count (5,000 to 15,000/mcL [5 to 15 × 10 9 /L] and an absolute neutrophil count ≤ 4000/mcL [≤ 4 × 10 9 /L]) Normal inflammatory marker levels (procalcitonin ≤ 0.5 ng/mL [≤ 0.5 mcg/L] and/or CRP ≤ 2 mg/dL [≤ 20 mg/L]) Normal urinalysis (and CSF analysis and chest radiograph, if done)

claims.text: Low-risk infants still get blood and urine cultures; some experts defer the lumbar puncture.
claims.quote: Blood and urine cultures should be obtained. Some experts defer lumbar puncture in infants who meet the above criteria

claims.text: Not fully immunized, fever > 39° C, no source: CBC with differential, blood culture, urinalysis and urine culture; chest X-ray if WBC ≥ 20,000/mcL.
claims.quote: Well-appearing children in this age group who have a temperature > 39° C and no identifiable source on examination (fever without source) and who are not fully immunized have a risk of occult bacteremia as high as 5% (equal to the risk before the pneumococcal and H. influenzae conjugate vaccines came into use). These children should have a complete blood count with differential, blood culture, and urinalysis and urine culture. A chest radiograph should be done if the WBC count is ≥ 20,000/mcL (≥ 20 × 10 9 /L) .
